intro: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never… These small words say how often you do something. They go with the present simple very often, and their position in the sentence is important.
objectifs: Know the adverbs of frequency and put them in order from 100% to 0%.
Put them in the right place: before the main verb, but after “to be”.
Use frequency expressions (every day, twice a week, once a month) at the end of the sentence.
Ask and answer questions with “How often…?” and “Do you ever…?”.

texte: Adverbs of frequency say how many times an action happens. The percentages in the table are not exact: they help you compare the words.
“Never” is already negative: don't use it with “don't”. “Hardly ever” (almost never) is more common in speaking than “rarely” or “seldom”, which are more formal.

lignes: They sometimes go to the cinema.

sections.note: “Normally” and “generally” mean the same as “usually” and go in the same place.

texte: In many languages the adverb goes after the verb. In English, it goes BEFORE the main verb: I often eat. This is the most common mistake.
With he / she / it, the verb keeps its -s: She often eats. The adverb doesn't change the verb.
In a negative sentence with don't / doesn't, the adverb goes after the auxiliary: I don't often go out.
exemples: I usually get up at seven.
We sometimes play football on Sundays.

sections.titre: After “to be” and between two verbs
texte: With the verb “to be”, it is the opposite: the adverb goes AFTER am / is / are. She is always late. They are never tired.
When there is an auxiliary or a modal (have got, can, will…), the adverb goes between it and the main verb: I can never remember his name. I've always got my phone with me.
Summary: subject + be + adverb; subject + adverb + verb; subject + auxiliary + adverb + verb.

lignes: I can never find my keys.

exemples: The bus is usually on time.
I'm never sure about the answer.

sections.titre: Usually, sometimes, often at the start or end
texte: To make them stronger, “sometimes”, “usually”, “normally” and “often” can also go at the start of the sentence, and “sometimes” can go at the end. “Always”, “never”, “rarely” and “hardly ever” don't go at the start in normal style.
So don't say “Always I go…” or “Never I eat…”.
exemples: Usually, the shop is quiet in the morning.
I go to the gym sometimes.

texte: For an exact frequency, use an expression with several words: every day, every week, once a week, twice a month, three times a year. These go at the end of the sentence (sometimes at the start), never between the subject and the verb.
Say “twice a week”: “a” means “in each”. “Per week” is more formal or technical. For two times, say “twice”; from three, say “three times, four times”.
To ask about frequency: “How often do you…?”. To ask if something happens at all: “Do you ever…?” (ever = at any time, in questions).
exemples: How often do you go swimming? — Twice a week.
I visit my grandparents once a month.
Do you ever cook? — Yes, sometimes. / No, never.
We go to Kribi every summer.

formule: subject + always / usually / often / sometimes / never + verb · subject + be + adverb · How often…? — once / twice / three times a week
prononciation: “often” is /ˈɒfn/ (silent t) or /ˈɒftən/: both are correct. American: /ˈɔːfn/.
“usually” /ˈjuːʒuəli/: stress on the first syllable, with the /ʒ/ sound of “television”. In fast speech: /ˈjuːʒli/.
“always” /ˈɔːlweɪz/: stress on AL-, and say the l lightly.
“twice” /twaɪs/ rhymes with “nice”. “once” is /wʌns/, with a w sound at the start, like “one”.
In “How often…?”, your voice goes down at the end, because it is a Wh- question.
erreurs: I go always to work by bus.
I always go to work by bus.
The adverb goes before the main verb.
With “to be”, the adverb goes after the verb.
Keep the -s for he / she / it after the adverb.
I play tennis two times by week.
I play tennis twice a week.
Two times = twice; in each week = a week.
A frequency expression doesn't go between the verb and its object: put it at the end.
“Always” doesn't go at the start of the sentence.

dialogue.contexte: A fitness coach in Ottawa asks a new client about her habits.
lignes: So, Émilie, how often do you do sport?
Not very often. I go swimming once a week, usually on Saturday.
OK. Do you ever walk to work?
Sometimes, in summer. But in winter I always take the bus. It's too cold!
And what about food? Do you often eat fast food?
No, I hardly ever eat fast food. But I'm often hungry at night.
Not really. I never go to bed before midnight.
OK. Let's start with three short walks a week.

mots: I call my mother once a week.
We go to the market twice a week.
Do you ever go to the theatre?
My morning routine is very simple.
the things you usually do, in the same order

exercices.consigne: Write the right adverb for each percentage: always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never.

exercices.titre: 2. Put the adverb in the right place
exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the adverb in brackets in the right place.
items: I drink tea in the morning. (usually)
I usually drink tea in the morning.
They rarely go to the cinema.
We are never late for class.
He doesn't usually work on Fridays.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I go often to the market.
I often go to the market.
My brother usually play football on Sundays.
My brother usually plays football on Sundays.
How many often do you visit them?
How often do you visit them?

exercices.consigne: Use the words to write a correct sentence or question.
items: They are often late. / They're often late.
how often / you / do sport? — 3 times a week
How often do you do sport? — Three times a week.

exercices.consigne: Write five true sentences about your habits with five different adverbs or expressions of frequency (one sentence with “to be”).
items: I always have coffee at breakfast. I usually walk to work. I'm often tired on Friday evenings. I go to the cinema once a month. I never watch TV in the morning.

a_retenir: always > usually > often > sometimes > rarely > hardly ever > never.
Before the main verb (I often eat), but after “to be” (I'm often late).
Never is already negative: I never eat meat, not “I don't never”.
Exact frequency at the end: once a week, twice a month, three times a year, every day.
Questions: How often do you…? / Do you ever…?
